title: Sword Guard (Tsuba)

altText: A flat, rounded iron plate with a central opening, decorated with metal inlay and a design including a dragon.

context: A tsuba, or sword guard, made in Japan in the early 18th century from iron with gold and copper. A tsuba sits between the blade and the handle of a Japanese sword, and in the long peaceful Edo period makers turned these small metal plates into detailed works of art. The museum's record tags this one with a dragon.

descriptions.k: This is a flat metal piece from a Japanese sword. It is called a tsuba. It is round and dark, with a hole in the middle. Shiny gold and copper decorate it. A dragon is part of the design. Can you find it?
descriptions.g12: This round metal plate is a tsuba, the part of a Japanese sword that sits between the handle and the blade. It is made of iron, with gold and copper added. A dragon is part of the design. Artists made tsuba beautiful even though they are small. What shapes can you find?
descriptions.g35: A tsuba sits between the blade and handle of a Japanese sword. This one, made in the early 1700s, is iron decorated with gold and copper, and a dragon is part of its design. Japan was at peace for much of this time, and tsuba became small works of art that showed taste. Look carefully at the way different metals share the surface. Why would an artist decorate something so small?
descriptions.g68: Made in the early 18th century, this tsuba is iron with gold and copper added. A tsuba kept the sword hand from sliding onto the blade, but in the peaceful Edo period it also became a showpiece of metalwork. Mixing metals lets a maker create contrast of color and texture on a small disk. Dragons in East Asian art are often tied to water, power, and good fortune. Which details on this piece show the maker's skill?
descriptions.g910: This tsuba shows how an item with a practical role developed into a refined art form. In the Edo period, when samurai often served as officials, swords became signs of status and taste, and fittings were made with artistic ambition. Here iron is combined with gold and copper to create contrast of tone, texture, and shine, and the dragon motif draws on East Asian traditions of power and protection. Consider how the circular format governs composition.
descriptions.g1112: The tsuba illustrates how function and art intertwine in Edo-period Japan. As the samurai's role shifted in a long era of peace, sword fittings such as this iron-gold-copper guard became vehicles for display, taste, and technical ingenuity. Dragon imagery had rich associations across East Asia, but how a particular owner read it is rarely recorded. The small circular format imposes tight compositional discipline, and the combination of metals suggests specialized workshop skill. How do we read an object whose original purpose is tied to weapons yet whose surviving significance is largely aesthetic?

teacherNote.context: A tsuba (sword guard) of iron with gold and copper, early 18th century, Edo period. It is the part that sits between the blade and the handle; in a long peaceful era such fittings became prized for artistry.
directions: Focus on craft and design: ask students to draw a pattern to fit a round disc with a central hole.
Discuss why objects connected to weapons can still be studied as design and craft, and how to talk about them respectfully.
Compare how dragons appear in this object and in other cultures' art.
